item.title: Palestinian journalist returns home after 15 months in Israeli detention
item.description:
Palestinian journalist returns home after 15 months in Israeli detention

Palestinian journalist Farah Abu Ayyash has returned home to her family following 450 days of detention in Israeli prisons, according to a report by the Islamic Republic News Agency (Irna).

Abu Ayyash, a West Bank correspondent for Iran's Tasnim News Agency, was freed on Thursday night after the Ofer Prison military court ordered her release, dismissing the charges brought against her after she served 15 months under administrative detention.

According to Irna, Abu Ayyash was initially detained on 6 August 2025, during an overnight military raid on her family home in Beit Ummar, north of Hebron. The outlet reported that her arrest was tied to her journalistic work covering local developments across the southern West Bank for Tasnim.

The report further noted that repeated procedural delays prolonged her case, keeping her detained without formal resolution under administrative detention at Damon Prison. Irna also reported that the correspondent was allegedly subjected to torture and mistreatment while in custody.

item.title: 'We must be so strong that no dares covet our land', Pezeshkian says
item.description:
'We must be so strong that no dares covet our land', Pezeshkian says

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has reminded his countrymen that “we must be so strong that no one dares to covet our land and identity”.

In a post on X marking forthcoming National Youth Day on 8 November, Pezeshkian recalled the "courage of Mohammad Hossein Fahmideh", a 13-year-old Iranian boy killed during the Iran-Iraq war, and paid tribute to children killed in Minab, Lamerd and other parts of the country.

Pezeshkian said: "The names and memories of our children remain in our minds and shape our collective historical memory, so that we know we must be so strong that no one dares to covet our land and identity."

item.title: Hormuz shipping traffic remains 70% below pre-war levels, UKMTO says
item.description:
Hormuz shipping traffic remains 70% below pre-war levels, UKMTO says

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains 70 percent below pre-conflict levels, with vessels continuing to face attacks, navigation interference and security risks across the Gulf, according to a weekly assessment by the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

A total of 277 vessel transits were recorded in the strait during the seven days to October 28, comprising 155 inbound and 122 outbound movements. The combined figure, which includes automatic identification system (AIS) observations and US-reported facilitated transits, was approximately 70 percent below pre-conflict levels.

UKMTO said AIS-observed transits increased to 64 from 47 the previous week, while US-reported facilitated movements remained broadly stable. The US Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS) estimates that about 80% of transits through the strait involve energy carriers.

Most vessels broadcasting AIS continued to use the Iranian route, although UKMTO reported an increase in traffic along the southern route.

The maritime monitoring body said it had recorded 88 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began on February 28, with the data suggesting at least 35 attacks on shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz in October, making it the worst month for attacks since the start of the war.

March was the second-worst month, with about 30 attacks, according to UKMTO data.

item.title: The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare
item.description:
The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia

The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas.

The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia.

item.title: Alaska prosecutor investigates alleged Democratic plot to confuse voters with second Dan Sullivan
item.description:
Mary Peltola denies knowledge as party accused of recruiting spoiler candidate with same name as sitting Republican

  • Alaska Senate race: what to know about Democrats’ alleged ballot-stacking effort

The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal and a civil investigation into an alleged scheme by Democrats to confuse voters by recruiting a spoiler candidate on the ballot for US Senate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, senator Dan Sullivan.

Speaking at a news conference in Anchorage on Friday, US attorney Michael Heyman cited reporting by the New York Times which suggested that the Senate campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola and national Democrats had, in his words, “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J Sullivan as a sham candidate”.

BP’s quarterly profits have been labelled “obscene” after they hit an 18-year high of $8.46bn (£6.3bn), as the war in the Middle East drove up oil and gas prices.

The energy company hailed a “banner quarter” on Friday, with its underlying ​replacement ⁠cost profit – a key measure of its income – almost quadrupling in the three months to the end of September, from $2.2bn in the same period ​a year ​ago. The jump meant BP’s quarterly profits hit their highest level since the $8.9bn recorded in 2008.
